Who We Are

Home-based care,
the way it should feel.

AllyCare Group specialises in bringing clinical excellence directly into your home. We believe the best place to heal, recover, and be cared for is in the comfort and familiarity of your own environment — surrounded by family.

We provide short and long-term home-based care solutions to individuals, families, care homes, nursing homes, and healthcare institutions across Kenya — delivered by locally and internationally qualified professionals.

Cancer & Palliative Care

You Don't Have to Care for Them Alone

AllyCare Clinical Team · Long-Term Care Programme

A cancer diagnosis changes everything for a family — not just for the person who is unwell, but for whoever quietly becomes their caregiver overnight. If that's you right now, here's what we've learned about supporting families through this, and how home-based care can carry some of the weight.

If someone you love has been diagnosed with cancer, you're probably tired in a way that's hard to explain to people who haven't been through it. Between hospital visits, medication schedules, and simply trying to hold everyone together, it's easy to feel like there's no room left to catch your breath. You are not alone in this, and more importantly — you don't have to carry it all yourself.

Cancer touches a great many Kenyan families. It's become one of the more common serious illnesses households here are navigating, and thankfully, awareness and access to care have grown a lot in recent years. Kenya now has a national palliative care policy specifically built to make sure people can get compassionate, pain-free care close to home. Pain medication that was once locked away and hard to access is now far more available through public health facilities. Slowly, the system is shifting toward recognising that healing — and comfort — often happen best where a person feels safest: at home, surrounded by family.

Why home matters so much during cancer care

Research with Kenyan families caring for a loved one through advanced cancer tells a consistent story: most of this care already happens at home, carried quietly by a spouse, a daughter, a son. And many of these caregivers say the same thing — they wish someone had walked alongside them. Not taken over, just walked alongside. Knowing how to manage pain at 2am, recognising when a symptom needs urgent attention versus when it can wait until morning, simply having someone to call — these are the things that turn an unbearable season into a manageable one.

How AllyCare walks with your family through this

This is exactly why our long-term care programme was built the way it is — not as a single service, but as a full circle of support around your household:

  • Home Health Care — a licensed nurse who understands pain relief, wound care, and what to watch for after chemotherapy, visiting on a rhythm that fits your loved one's treatment.
  • AllyCare Pharmacies — medications delivered to your door, with a pharmacist who checks that everything works safely together, so that's one less thing on your mind.
  • CareMax Essentials — the everyday supplies, like incontinence care and dressings, arriving reliably so you're never caught without them.
  • AllyRide | MediRide — a gentle, nurse-accompanied ride to chemotherapy or radiotherapy, and safe transfers home after a hospital stay, so getting there is never the reason a session is missed.
  • Support for you, the caregiver — because we know the person caring for a cancer patient needs care too. Our team trains and checks in with families, not just patients.

If your loved one has recently been discharged from hospital, that's often the moment families feel most unsure of what comes next. It's a good time to have a conversation with us — before things feel urgent, not after.

Grounded in national cancer care data and research from IARC/GLOBOCAN, Kenya's National Cancer Control Strategy, the Kenya Palliative Care Policy, and caregiver studies from Kenyan hospices and palliative care units.

Alzheimer's & Dementia Care

When a Parent Starts to Forget

AllyCare Clinical Team · Long-Term Care Programme

It often starts small — a missed name, a repeated question, a familiar road that suddenly feels unfamiliar. If you've noticed these changes in someone you love, here's what Kenyan families and researchers have learned, and how gentle, in-home support can make all the difference.

There's a particular kind of ache that comes with watching a parent or grandparent slowly become less like themselves. It's confusing, it's often lonely, and in many Kenyan homes, it's a journey families walk quietly, without quite knowing what's happening or who to turn to. If this sounds familiar, please know — what you're noticing has a name, it's more common than you might think, and there is real support available.

Memory and cognitive changes in older adults are more widespread across Kenya than most families realise, and that number is expected to grow as our population ages. Yet unlike many other health conditions, dementia is still often mistaken for simply "getting old," which means families frequently go years without a clear answer — and without the tools to cope well. Kenyan researchers have found that stigma, and a general lack of awareness, are some of the biggest reasons families delay getting help, even when they sense something isn't right.

You're not imagining it, and you're not failing

Almost all dementia caregiving in Kenya falls on family — usually a spouse or an adult child — and it is genuinely hard work, emotionally and practically. If you've felt exhausted, uncertain, or even guilty for feeling overwhelmed, that is an entirely normal response to an enormous responsibility, not a sign that you're doing anything wrong. The encouraging news is that community-based screening efforts across Kenya have shown that simply getting a trained professional into the home — early, gently, without pressure — makes a real difference in how families cope and how well their loved one is supported going forward.

How AllyCare supports families navigating memory loss

Our approach is built around steady, familiar routines and a team that gets to know your parent as a person, not just a diagnosis:

  • Home Health Care — nurses and caregivers trained to move gently through confusion or agitation, keep daily routines consistent, and reduce fall risk around the home.
  • Everyday structure and companionship — light activity, conversation, and nutrition support woven into a steady daily rhythm, which genuinely helps people living with memory loss feel more secure.
  • ACMG Equipments — mobility aids, hospital beds, and safety fittings assessed and fitted for your specific home, so the space feels safer without feeling clinical.
  • A break for you — scheduled respite care so you can rest, and honest, practical guidance on how to communicate and stay safe day to day.
  • AllyRide | MediRide — calm, familiar transport to memory clinic visits, so appointments feel less disorienting for your loved one.

If something feels different about a parent or relative lately, trust that instinct. An in-home assessment isn't a big, scary step — it's simply a conversation, in the comfort of your own home, about what support could look like for your family.

Informed by dementia research from the Global Burden of Disease study, community screening programmes across rural Kenya, the STRiDE Kenya dementia situation report, and lived-experience studies from Aga Khan University, Nairobi.

Post-Surgery Recovery

Healing Doesn't End at the Hospital Doors

AllyCare Clinical Team · Long-Term Care Programme

The operation is over, the discharge papers are signed, and suddenly you're home — with a wound to watch, medication to manage, and a hundred small worries you didn't have yesterday. That transition is harder than it should be. Here's how thoughtful home support changes it.

There's a strange quiet that settles over a household in the days after someone comes home from surgery. The relief of leaving the hospital is real, but so is the uncertainty that follows it — is this normal swelling or something to worry about, is it too soon to shower, did we get the medication timing right? Families are rarely given more than a rushed set of instructions on the way out the door, and then left to figure the rest out on their own.

This isn't unique to any one hospital or any one family. Research into surgical discharge across the region tells a familiar story: patients are often sent home with genuine goodwill from their care team, but without the follow-up support that turns good instructions into confident, safe recovery. Studies from teaching hospitals here in Kenya have found that while many nurses do take time to counsel patients before discharge, that guidance rarely continues once the patient is actually home — and it's in those early days at home, not in the hospital ward, where most complications and readmissions quietly begin.

Why the first weeks at home matter so much

Healing is not a single event that happens in an operating theatre — it's a process that continues for weeks, sometimes months, largely unseen and mostly at home. A wound that looks fine on day two can look different by day five. Pain that isn't well managed can quietly stop someone from doing the deep breathing or gentle movement their body actually needs to recover well. And medication schedules — often several new prescriptions at once — are surprisingly easy to get wrong when you're tired, sore, and trying to remember everything the doctor said in a five-minute conversation.

How AllyCare supports a safer recovery at home

This is precisely the gap our home-based recovery care is designed to close — a team that picks up exactly where the hospital left off:

  • Home Health Care — a nurse who checks the wound properly, changes dressings with a trained eye for early signs of infection, and knows when something needs a doctor's attention versus when it's simply part of healing.
  • Medication and pain management — someone keeping track of what to take and when, so recovery isn't slowed down by missed doses or preventable discomfort.
  • Mobility and daily support — gentle help with moving, bathing, and everyday tasks in those first fragile days, reducing the risk of falls or overexertion.
  • AllyCare Pharmacies — prescriptions delivered to your door, so there's no need to make a tiring trip to the pharmacy while you're still healing.
  • AllyRide | MediRide — comfortable transport for follow-up appointments and suture removal, without the stress of arranging transport while still recovering.

If you or someone you love has a procedure coming up, the best time to think about home support isn't the day of discharge — it's before you ever walk into the operating theatre. A little preparation now can spare you a very difficult first week later.

Informed by research on surgical discharge and home-care experiences from Kenyatta National Hospital and regional teaching hospitals, alongside established post-operative and wound-care nursing guidance.

Stroke Recovery

Getting Life Back, One Day at a Time

AllyCare Clinical Team · Long-Term Care Programme

A stroke can change a family in an instant — and the road back is rarely straightforward. If you're supporting someone relearning how to walk, speak, or simply feel like themselves again, here's what we've learned about making that journey gentler.

Nothing quite prepares a family for the moment a stroke changes everything. One day someone is independent, and the next, they may need help with the most basic parts of daily life — sitting up, speaking clearly, holding a cup. It's disorienting for the person going through it, and it's exhausting for the people around them trying to help, often without any real guidance on where to begin.

Across our region, stroke is becoming an increasingly common part of family life, and it tends to affect people earlier here than it does elsewhere in the world. What's especially difficult is that specialist stroke rehabilitation — the kind of structured physiotherapy, speech therapy, and occupational therapy that helps someone regain lost function — remains genuinely hard to access. Kenya has very few specialist stroke units, and most people are discharged home within a short time of their hospital stay. Research from Kenyan hospitals has found that many families receive little to no formal education on stroke care before their loved one comes home, and are simply left to learn as they go.

Why home becomes the real rehabilitation ground

Here is the encouraging part of the research: recovery after stroke happens gradually, and family involvement matters enormously. Studies following stroke survivors in Kenya and neighbouring countries have found that those who continue structured rehabilitation and receive consistent support at home tend to regain far more independence in the months that follow than those who don't. Family caregivers — often daughters, wives, or mothers — become the quiet engine of that recovery, but they carry a heavy, often invisible load, especially without training in how to safely assist with movement, communication, or the emotional ups and downs that come with relearning basic life skills.

How AllyCare supports stroke recovery at home

We built our long-term care programme around exactly this gap — steady, skilled support that continues long after the hospital stay ends:

  • Home Health Care — nurses experienced in stroke after-care: monitoring blood pressure and medication, watching for warning signs of a second stroke, and supporting safe movement and positioning.
  • Physiotherapy support — guided mobility and strength-building exercises woven into everyday routine, helping regain independence step by step rather than all at once.
  • Patient and family training — practical, hands-on guidance for the household on safe transfers, communication techniques, and how to support recovery without doing everything for your loved one.
  • ACMG Equipments — wheelchairs, walking aids, and hospital beds fitted to the home, adjusted as ability improves over time.
  • AllyRide | MediRide — safe, unhurried transport to follow-up neurology and rehabilitation appointments, removing one more obstacle from an already demanding routine.

Recovery from stroke is rarely a straight line — there will be good days and harder ones. What matters most is that your family isn't navigating it in isolation. With the right support at home, small wins compound, and independence, however partial, has real room to return.

Informed by stroke epidemiology and rehabilitation research from Kenyan referral hospitals, community-based stroke care studies in East Africa, and the World Stroke Organization's regional reporting on stroke care in Kenya.
